nodes.title: The ARC
nodes.summary: ZFS's reading cache—the reason your machine's memory looks full, and why that's the system working, not leaking.

nodes.title: Ashift
nodes.summary: ZFS's recorded guess about a disk's true cell size—made once, when a disk team is created, and permanent forever. The one setting a wrong guess makes unfixable. Use 12.

nodes.title: Checksums
nodes.summary: A tiny fingerprint for every piece of data, re-checked on every read—so a lying disk gets caught in the act. Noticing damage is guaranteed; fixing it needs a spare copy.

nodes.title: Compression
nodes.summary: Squeezing data used to cost speed to save space. ZFS's method is so fast the trade runs backward—leave it on, and it often makes things faster.

nodes.title: Copy-on-Write
nodes.summary: ZFS never writes over existing data—every change lands on fresh space first, then takes effect in one clean switch. The habit everything else stands on.
entry_points: why does zfs not need fsck

nodes.title: Datasets
nodes.summary: A named slice of the pool that looks like a folder but carries its own rules—its own settings, limits, and history. Costs nothing to make. Make many.
entry_points: how many datasets should i make

nodes.title: Deduplication
nodes.summary: Storing each duplicate piece of data only once—sounds free, actually costs a standing memory tax on every write, forever. Plain compression wins in almost every home setup.

nodes.title: The ECC Question
nodes.summary: "ZFS without special error-checking memory will eat your data" is the loudest myth in ZFS—it doesn't survive inspection, per the co-creator himself.
entry_points: do i need ecc ram for zfs

nodes.title: A Short History of Filesystems
nodes.summary: Fifty years in one story: each generation of filesystems answers the previous generation's disaster—ending (so far) at the generation ZFS opened, which stopped trusting the disk itself.
entry_points: why are there so many filesystems

nodes.title: The Filesystem Landscape
nodes.summary: The filesystems you actually meet—ext4, XFS, NTFS, APFS, Btrfs—one honest line each, and the specific combination ZFS offers that the others don't.

nodes.title: Your First Pool
nodes.summary: Creating a pool is one command and four judgments—two of them permanent (how the disks are teamed, and the disk cell-size setting), the rest changeable over coffee.

nodes.title: The Free-Space Discipline
nodes.summary: On ZFS, empty space isn't spare room—it's the workshop floor every change is made on. Fill the pool and it gets permanently grumpier.
entry_points: how full can a zfs pool get

nodes.title: L2ARC
nodes.summary: A second-tier cache on a fast drive—not free speed, because indexing it spends the memory cache that's actually fast. A measured fix for a proven problem, not an upgrade.
entry_points: should i add a cache drive

nodes.title: Mirrors
nodes.summary: Two or more disks holding identical copies of everything—half the space, in exchange for the best speed, the fastest recovery, and the most freedom to change your mind later.

nodes.title: Mountpoints
nodes.summary: Where a dataset appears in your folders is a setting stored on the dataset itself—the location travels with the data, not with the machine.

nodes.title: The Pool
nodes.summary: All your disks, combined into one shared pot of storage—and the surprise inside the word: the pool itself keeps no spare copies.

nodes.title: Import and Export
nodes.summary: The pool's entire self-description lives on its member disks—any machine with OpenZFS can import them and get everything, mounts included. Data was never married to the machine.
entry_points: motherboard died is my data safe

nodes.title: Property Inheritance
nodes.summary: Settings flow downhill: set once on a parent dataset, every child follows until one is told otherwise. There is no central settings file—the tree is the settings.

nodes.title: ZFS Under Proxmox
nodes.summary: What the Proxmox installer actually built: a pool for the operating system, a raw virtual disk per VM, and a cache that shares memory with your machines—the most common accidental ZFS, decoded.

nodes.title: RAIDZ
nodes.summary: Protection by recovery math instead of full copies—more usable space than mirrors, but a RAIDZ team moves at one disk's pace for scattered small requests. Big libraries, not virtual machines.

nodes.title: RAIDZ Expansion
nodes.summary: Adding one more disk to an existing RAIDZ team—impossible for a decade, possible since early 2025, with fine print about how much space you actually get back.
entry_points: can i add a disk to raidz

nodes.title: Recordsize
nodes.summary: The size of the chunks ZFS stores files in—adjustable per dataset. It matters when programs change small pieces inside huge files, and changing it only affects files written afterward.

nodes.title: Replacing a Disk
nodes.summary: The procedure you'll run under stress, made boring: identify by serial, replace, watch the resilver, scrub. The real risk is precision, not speed.
entry_points: disk died what do i do
how to replace a failed disk

nodes.title: Resilvering
nodes.summary: How ZFS refills a replacement disk—copying only real data, checking every piece as it goes. A half-full pool recovers in half the time, and the time matters.

nodes.title: Rollback
nodes.summary: Not timeline navigation—demolition. Rolling back to Tuesday destroys everything after Tuesday, permanently. Clones and .zfs/snapshot are the gentle paths.

nodes.title: Sanoid and Syncoid
nodes.summary: Not one "backup system"—two small helpers: sanoid takes and prunes snapshots on a schedule; syncoid ships them to another machine. Both just automate things you can do by hand.

nodes.title: Scrubs
nodes.summary: A scheduled read-through of everything the pool holds, so quiet damage in untouched data gets found while a spare copy still exists to fix it. Finding is guaranteed; fixing isn't.

nodes.title: Send and Receive
nodes.summary: How a frozen moment travels to another machine—an exact copy, and after the first trip, only what changed. Not a file-comparing sync tool: it already knows what's different.
entry_points: how to copy a dataset to another machine

nodes.title: Snapshots
nodes.summary: A frozen moment of a dataset that copies nothing—it just keeps the past from being thrown away. Free to take; the cost arrives slowly, as the present drifts from the moment you kept.

nodes.title: Snapshots and Disappearing Space
nodes.summary: You deleted the files and the free space barely moved—because snapshots are still holding those files. The space changed owners; it didn't come back.
entry_points: deleted files but no space freed

nodes.title: Snapshots Are Not Backups
nodes.summary: A snapshot lives on the same disks, in the same pool, behind the same mistakes as the data. It's the versioning half of a backup strategy; replication is the other half.
entry_points: do i need backups with zfs

nodes.title: The Vdev
nodes.summary: The small team of disks that back each other up—where protection actually lives, and therefore where failure actually lives. Lose one whole team, lose the whole pool.

nodes.title: What a Filesystem Is
nodes.summary: The absolute ground floor: a disk stores only numbered blocks and has no idea what a file is—the filesystem is the ledger that invents files, names, and folders on top of them.

nodes.title: What ZFS Is
nodes.summary: A system for storing data built around one promise: what you put in comes back exactly—or ZFS tells you, loudly, instead of silently handing you something broken.

nodes.title: ZIL and SLOG
nodes.summary: Not a fast lane for writes—a diary of promises, written constantly and read exactly once: after a crash. A SLOG just moves the diary to a faster drive, and only promise-me-now writes ever use it.

nodes.title: Reading zpool status
nodes.summary: The pool's one health report—and DEGRADED means the design is working, not that the pool is dying. How to read it without panic.

nodes.title: Zvols
nodes.summary: A slice of the pool that pretends to be a blank disk instead of a folder— what virtual machines get handed. Still checked, snapshotted, and copied like everything else.
